raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old man presented with a seven-day history of fatigue, fever, and jaundice. He initially went to a nearby clinic as symptoms worsened. Subsequently, he was also diagnosed with AKI and transferred to our hospital. He had no contact with rats and did not do field work. He had no prior medical history.
Vital signs at the time of visit were as follows: blood pressure 116/73 mmHg, pulse 110/min, body temperature 37.4 C, and respiration rate 18/min. His ocular conjunctivae wereyellow-tinged and congested. His oral cavity was not swollen or reddish; however, he complained of a sore throat.
Blood tests revealed a white blood cell count of 18900/muL. His hemoglobin was 10.8 g/dL and platelet count was 2.6 x 104/muL, and no schizocytes were observed. Aspartate aminotransferase was 31 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 18 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 234 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 340 U/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase 41 U/L, total bilirubin 12.4 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 10.5 mg/dL, which is above the threshold for hyperbilirubinemia. Blood urea nitrogen was 85.6 mg/dL, creatinine was 8.3 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein was elevated to 29.26 mg/dL (normal range 0.0-0.3 mg/dL). In urine qualitative assays, positive results were observed for proteins, urobilinogen, bilirubin, and occult blood. In addition, urine sugar was positive despite not having diabetes. Chest CT showed multiple nodules in both lungs (Figure 1). Abdominal CT showed no abnormality that could explain the jaundice and kidney failure.
We initially strongly suspected leptospirosis. However, other infectious diseases could not be excluded because the multiple nodules in the lungs were atypical for leptospirosis.
Because there was a possibility of various diseases, we avoided IV penicillin and started IV piperacillin-tazobactam and minocycline instead. He became anuric and was started on urgent hemodialysis on the second hospital day. Later on, antibody and PCR assays for Leptospira were negative. F. necrophorum was isolated in blood cultures on the second day. Further late, Streptococcus intermedius were isolated in blood cultures on the seventh day. We diagnosed his main disease as F. necrophorum rather than S. intermedius bacteremia based on the past case reports and the speed of positive blood cultures. Since F. necrophorum is famous for Lemierre's syndrome, we performed ultrasound in his jugular vein but found no thrombus. In addition, the dentist diagnosed a minor periodontal infection. F. necrophorum is thought to spread from periodontal infections. The main pathogen was F. necrophorum, but other anaerobic bacteria were also suspected to be involved. In addition, we were not able to test the susceptibility of F. necrophorum to penicillin. His treatment was thus de-escalated to IV ceftriaxone (CTRX) 1 g every 24 h and metronidazole (MNZ) 500 mg every 12 h on the 3rd day. Later, MNZ was increased up to 500 mg every 6 h. These treatments were continued up to the 17th day. The multiple lung nodules formed cavities and later disappeared after definitive therapy (Figure 2). He responded well to the treatment, was taken off hemodialysis, and discharged on the 18th hospital day. After discharge, he continued the treatment with amoxicillin and MNZ orally for three weeks (Figure 3). He had no relapse after three months of follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old man presented with a 7-day history of fatigue, fever, sore throat, and progressive jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially visited a local clinic after 7 days of worsening fatigue, fever, sore throat, and jaundice, where he was found to have acute kidney injury and was transferred to a tertiary hospital.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical history; denied contact with rats or agricultural field work (subsequently found on inpatient dental exam to have a minor periodontal infection).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fatigue, fever, sore throat, jaundice, and subsequent anuria.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: blood pressure 116/73 mmHg, pulse 110 beats/min, temperature 37.4 °C, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. Ocular conjunctivae were icteric and congested; oral cavity showed no pharyngeal swelling or erythema, though dental examination identified minor periodontal disease.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: WBC 18,900/µL, Hb 10.8 g/dL, platelets 2.6 × 10⁴/µL (no schistocytes on smear), AST 31 U/L, ALT 18 U/L, LDH 234 U/L, ALP 340 U/L, GGT 41 U/L, total bilirubin 12.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 10.5 mg/dL, BUN 85.6 mg/dL, creatinine 8.3 mg/dL, and CRP 29.26 mg/dL (ref 0.0–0.3 mg/dL). Urinalysis was positive for protein, urobilinogen, bilirubin, occult blood, and glucose (normoglycemic renal glucosuria). Leptospira antibody and PCR assays were negative. Internal jugular vein Doppler ultrasound showed no thrombosis.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules that subsequently cavitated; abdominal CT showed no hepatobiliary obstruction. Blood cultures isolated Fusobacterium necrophorum on hospital day 2 and Streptococcus intermedius on hospital day 7.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed odontogenic Fusobacterium necrophorum and Streptococcus intermedius polymicrobial bacteremia mimicking Weil's disease with septic pulmonary emboli, severe thrombocytopenia, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and anuric acute kidney injury (variant Lemierre's syndrome without jugular vein thrombosis); leptospirosis was excluded by negative Leptospira PCR and serology. Treated initially with empiric IV piperacillin-tazobactam, minocycline, and urgent hemodialysis (started on day 2 for anuria), then de-escalated on day 3 to IV ceftriaxone (1 g q24h) plus IV metronidazole (500 mg q12h, escalated to 500 mg q6h) through day 17. Renal function recovered off dialysis, cavitary lung nodules resolved, and he was discharged on day 18 to complete 3 weeks of oral amoxicillin and metronidazole without relapse at 3 months.
